title: Uruk (Warka)
summary: Uruk, the ruin field of Warka in southern Iraq, grew from a late-5th-millennium BCE settlement into perhaps the largest city of its age; its Eanna temple precinct yielded the oldest known writing, conventionally dated c. 3200 BCE.
card: Uruk lies in the desert of Iraq's Al-Muthanna Governorate, once on the edge of Euphrates marshes. In the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE) it held an estimated 20,000–50,000 people, temples on the Anu terrace and in the Eanna precinct, and the administrators who devised proto-cuneiform. Walled early in the 3rd millennium BCE, a wall later credited to Gilgamesh, it stayed inhabited into the 1st millennium CE and has been dug by German teams since 1912.
what:
Uruk is the ruin field known in Arabic as al-Warkāʾ, about 33 km east of As-Samawah in Iraq's Al-Muthanna Governorate. Its Sumerian name was Unug; Greek sources called it Orchoē, and it is also known as Erech. The city stood southwest of an ancient Euphrates channel, now dry, at the edge of freshwater marshes, with canals running through its quarters; the river's later shift away from the site was a key factor in its decline.

Settlement began around the end of the 5th millennium BCE, at the close of the Ubaid period, and grew through the 4th millennium, the span archaeologists call the Uruk period after this site. In the Late Uruk phase (c. 3350–3100 BCE) Uruk covered roughly 2.5 km², nearly twice the next largest settlement, and housed an estimated 20,000 to 50,000 people. In the west, a terrace raised at least ten times to about 12 m, the so-called Anu Ziggurat, carried the White Temple, a whitewashed hall of about 22 by 17.5 m whose construction is radiocarbon-dated to 3517–3358 BCE. To the east lay Eanna, precinct of the goddess Inanna, where about 5,000 proto-cuneiform tablets, the oldest known writing, were recovered, nearly all from rubbish used as building fill. Facades of the period's great mudbrick buildings were studded with painted clay cones set in mosaic patterns.

Early in the 3rd millennium BCE a mudbrick wall up to 5 m thick, with semicircular bastions, was built round the city; later tradition credited it to King Gilgamesh. Published figures for the city's size differ, from 2.5 km² to more than 6 km² and from 9.8 km to about 11 km of wall, because they describe different phases and methods. Uruk stayed a religious centre for millennia: a ziggurat was raised in Eanna about 4,200 years ago, the Seleucid-period city had great sanctuaries such as the Bit Resh of Anu and Antum and the Irigal of Ishtar, and a temple was built under Parthian rule. Occupation continued into the late Sasanian period (7th century CE). German teams have excavated the site since 1912, and in 2016 it was inscribed as part of the UNESCO World Heritage property The Ahwar of Southern Iraq.

uncertainty.note: Start: the DAI-led conservation report places the founding at the end of the 5th millennium BCE, while the ICOMOS evaluation gives the end of the Ubaid period, c. 3800 BCE; the record uses -3999 (4000 BCE) with ±200 years. End: ICOMOS gives the late Sasanian period, 7th century CE (printed '7rd'); the Artefacts/DAI reconstruction project says only 'to the 1st millennium CE'. The end year 650 is the midpoint of the 7th century, not an attested abandonment date.

how: Uruk grew on a marshy deltaic plain where the Euphrates, its channels and freshwater marshes supplied water, fish, reeds and fertile soil. Canals ran through the city from north to south, linking quarters to river traffic and watering gardens inside the walls. During the 4th millennium BCE the population swelled and institutions centred on the temple precincts came to control large stores of goods and labour; keeping track of production, rations and workers led administrators in Eanna to draw signs on clay, first with curved incised lines (Uruk IV) and about a century later with impressed, straightened strokes (Uruk III). The same script then appears at Jemdet Nasr, Khafajah and Tell Uqair, so the technique spread quickly through Babylonia. Builders worked almost wholly in earth: sun-dried earth blocks laid in mud mortar, horizontal layers of bitumen mortar as waterproofing in the Anu terrace, reed-mat reinforcement layers in the later Eanna ziggurat (about 11.5 million blocks), white lime paint on the White Temple and painted clay-cone mosaics on facades. The terrace that carried the White Temple was rebuilt and raised at least ten times. Early in the 3rd millennium a double ring of mudbrick wall with some burnt brick enclosed the city. Long-term decline followed the drying of the marshes after about 2000 BCE and the river's change of course, though the temples were rebuilt in Seleucid and Parthian times.
why_it_matters: Uruk is the clearest case in the archaeological record of a society crossing into urban life. Its administrators produced the oldest known writing, a bookkeeping system for grain, livestock, labour and rations; that script developed into cuneiform, which was later adapted to write Akkadian, Eblaite, Elamite, Hittite and other languages across the ancient Middle East and was still written in the 1st century CE, more than three thousand years after its invention. The city's scale, temple institutions, monumental mudbrick architecture and canal network set the pattern for the Sumerian city-states that followed, and objects in Uruk style reached from central Iran to the Nile Delta before about 3000 BCE. Uruk also supplied the setting of Mesopotamian literary memory: the Epic of Gilgamesh, among the earliest works of literature, centres on its king and his wall, and the Sumerian poem Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta claims the city invented writing. If the Eanna rubbish fills had not preserved some 5,000 archaic tablets, the earliest stage of writing would be known only from the slightly later Uruk III-type tablets found at northern Babylonian sites, and historians would have far weaker evidence that writing began as administration rather than literature. The site also shows how fragile early cities were: when the marshes dried and the Euphrates moved away, Uruk shrank to a sanctuary town and finally emptied. Today its eroding mudbrick ruins are part of Iraq's World Heritage property, conserved by Iraqi and German teams who still depend on clay from the region's canals to repair them.

related.because: The need of Uruk's temple administration to track goods, labour and rations led its officials to create proto-cuneiform, the earliest known writing, found in the Eanna precinct.
Farming, herding and the exploitation of marsh and river resources on the southern Mesopotamian plain produced the surpluses and dense populations from which a city of tens of thousands could grow.

perspectives.account: In the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE) Uruk had 20,000–50,000 people on about 2.5 km², nearly twice the next largest settlement, making it arguably the world's first true city.

perspectives.holder: Fassbinder, Ostner, Scheiblecker and van Ess (2018); Pleiades gazetteer; Seshat Databank
perspectives.account: By about 3000–2900 BCE the city held around 40,000–50,000 people and its walls enclosed some 5 km² (Fassbinder et al.) to more than 6 km² (Pleiades); these larger figures describe the walled city of the early 3rd millennium rather than the Late Uruk town.
Gilgamesh may have been a real king of Uruk around 2700 BCE, and tradition credits him with the city's great wall, though he became mainly a figure of later stories.

Gilgamesh, Enmerkar and Lugalbanda belong to a semi-mythological First Dynasty of Uruk (c. 2800–2700 BCE); the account of Enmerkar inventing writing is myth, though it agrees with the evidence that writing began at Uruk.

The conventional date of 3200 BCE for the first tablets is uncertain because they come from rubbish fills; one charcoal sample suggests 3500–3390 BCE but is a lone date, and new radiocarbon dating was under way.

phases.description: Settlement founded around the end of the 5th millennium BCE (end of the Ubaid period) and grows through the earlier Uruk period.
White Temple built on the much-rebuilt Anu terrace (radiocarbon 3517–3358 BCE); the terrace is raised at least ten times to about 12 m.
Late Uruk urban peak: about 2.5 km², Eanna and Anu districts in use, proto-cuneiform administration.
Double mudbrick city wall erected at the beginning of the 3rd millennium BCE and kept in use until at least the Seleucid period (3rd century BCE).
Eanna ziggurat raised, about 4,200 years before 2023 (approximate date from the conservation team).
Seleucid-period sacred complexes: Bit Resh of Anu and Antum beside the Anu ziggurat, the Irigal of Ishtar, the Bit Akitu, the Eanna ziggurat and the Karaindash temple.
Under Parthian rule (250 BCE–227 CE) the Temple of Charyos is built as the city enters its final decline.
Abandoned after the late Sasanian period (7th century CE); mudbrick ruins protected by sediment.
Excavated by the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft and then the DAI from 1912; the White Temple exposed in the 1930s and left unprotected for about 90 years.
Emergency conservation: overhangs of the Eanna ziggurat secured in 2018; White Temple walls sheathed in new earth blocks from autumn 2022 (partial conservation, not reconstruction).
